title: Combining conditions

curriculum.title: Combining Comparisons with and, or, not
curriculum.answer:
Sometimes one comparison is not enough. Combining conditions lets a program ask two questions in one test, so an if can check that a value lies between two limits or that two values differ. You join comparisons with and and or, and you flip a result with not.

Use `and` when every part must be true. Use `or` when at least one part must be true. Use `not` to reverse True and False. Comparisons are checked first, then `not`, then `and`, then `or`, so parentheses help make the order clear.

```python
x = 4
low = 3
high = 10
inside = x > low and x < high
print(inside)
```
```text
True
```
Here `x`, `low`, and `high` are all shown first. Then `x > low` is True and `x < high` is True, so `True and True` gives True. The program stores that result in `inside`.

```python
x = 2
y = 2
different = x < y or x > y
print(different)
if different:
    print("not equal")
else:
    print("equal")
```
```text
False
```
```text
equal
```
Both comparisons are False because 2 is neither less than nor greater than 2. `False or False` is False, so the `else` path runs and prints equal.

A common mistake is swapping them. A number cannot be both less than and greater than another number, so `x < y and x > y` is always False for not-equal. Another mistake is using `and` for an outside check: `x < low and x > high` cannot be True when low is at most high: one value cannot be below the lower limit and above the upper limit at once. Outside needs `or`, inside needs `and`.

units.title: Combining Comparisons with and or not
units.explanation: Two boundary comparisons can be joined with and to express strictly between. Use or for either outside boundary, and not to reverse a Boolean result. The examples compare numbers, so each comparison gives True or False.
units.opening_question: When should one if test check two comparisons at once?

quiz.prompt: What is the value of result?
quiz.code:
x = 1
y = 2
result = x < y or x > y
print(result)
options: False because both sides must be True
True because one side is True
False because and and or act the same
quiz.explanation: One side is True, so or gives True. The value needs only one True side.

quiz.prompt: Choose the test that prints inside only for a strictly interior value.
quiz.code:
x = 2
low = 3
high = 10
if ___:
    print("inside")
else:
    print("outside")
options: not x > low and x < high
quiz.explanation: Inside needs both bounds True together, so and joins them.

quiz.prompt: Why is this not-equal test wrong?
options: It means the same as or
It is always False because both sides cannot be True together
quiz.explanation: One pair of numbers cannot satisfy both directions, so and is never True here.

quiz.prompt: Choose the test that prints alarm only when x is outside the limits.
quiz.code:
x = 12
low = 3
high = 10
if ___:
    print("alarm")
else:
    print("ok")
quiz.explanation: 7 is between the limits, so the outside test is False. The bug joins outside tests with and, which cannot catch low-side values.

x = 1
y = 2
ok = x < y or x > y
print(ok)
ready = x > 0 and y > 5
print(ready)
print(not ready)
prediction.explanation: First or has one True side, so True. Second and has one False side, so False. not False is True.

exercise.title: Strictly Between Limits
exercise.instructions: Decide whether a reading is strictly between two limits. Inputs: x is the reading, low is the lower limit, high is the upper limit. Example: x=5, low=3, high=10 gives inside=True. Assign True or False to inside. Assume low is at most high.

fresh_exercise.title: Outside Limits Alarm
fresh_exercise.instructions: Decide whether a reading needs attention. Inputs: x is the reading, low is the lower limit, high is the upper limit. Alarm means the reading is outside the limits. Example: x=1, low=3, high=10 gives alarm=True. Assign True or False to alarm. Assume low is at most high.
